config.title: Build typed fetch client with endpoint map

intro.title: Build typed fetch client with endpoint map
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed fetch client in TypeScript that uses an endpoint map to organize API routes. You will learn how to define a TypeScript interface to describe the shape of your endpoint map, ensuring type safety for your API calls. The core concept involves using TypeScript's type system to create a reusable client that prevents errors by checking URLs and expected response types at compile time. You will work with async/await for handling promises, the fetch API for making HTTP requests, and generic types to keep your client flexible. By the end, you'll have a structured, type-safe way to manage all your API endpoints in one place.
intro.usecase: This typed fetch client pattern is essential in enterprise applications like e-commerce platforms, where you need to manage dozens of API endpoints for products, orders, users, and inventory. In a dashboard interface, each widget—sales charts, customer tables, inventory alerts—would use this client to fetch typed data from different endpoints while maintaining consistency. Frontend developers use this approach to prevent runtime errors when integrating with backend services, ensuring that API responses match the expected TypeScript interfaces. This pattern also simplifies maintenance in large codebases where multiple teams work on different API integrations.

objectives: Construct a typed endpoint map using TypeScript interfaces
Implement a generic fetch client function with type parameters
Configure type-safe request and response handling for API calls
Initialize the fetch client with endpoint-specific configurations
Apply the endpoint map to route API requests with proper typing
Manipulate type parameters to enforce data structure constraints
Integrate the typed fetch client into a sample application structure

steps.title: Import TypeScript and define base types
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript file and define an interface named ApiResponse with a generic type parameter T to represent the structure of API responses.
steps.hint: Start by creating an interface with a generic type parameter. The interface should have a 'data' property of type T and a 'status' property of type number.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a generic ApiResponse interface that can be used to type API responses throughout your fetch client.
successCriteria: An interface named ApiResponse with a generic type parameter T is defined, containing 'data: T' and 'status: number' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your interface has both 'data' and 'status' properties with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: create an interface named ApiResponse with a generic type parameter T that includes both data and status properties.

steps.title: Create endpoint map type definition
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript type named EndpointMap that maps endpoint names to their configuration using a mapped type. Each configuration should include method (string), path (string), and responseType (using the ApiResponse interface).
steps.hint: Use a mapped type like `type EndpointMap = { [key: string]: { method: string; path: string; responseType: ApiResponse } }` or similar.

steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a type definition that describes the shape of your API endpoint configuration map.
successCriteria: The EndpointMap type is defined with a mapped type structure, includes method, path, and responseType properties, and uses the ApiResponse interface for responseType.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your EndpointMap includes all required properties (method, path, responseType) and uses the ApiResponse interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: The EndpointMap type definition is missing or incorrect. Review the mapped type syntax and ensure it includes method, path, and responseType properties.

steps.title: Define concrete endpoint configurations
steps.instruction: Create a constant object named 'endpoints' that implements the EndpointMap type with specific API endpoints. Include at least two endpoints: one for fetching users and one for fetching posts.
steps.hint: Use the 'const' keyword to declare an object with properties that match the EndpointMap structure. Each property should have a 'url' string and a 'method' literal type.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a concrete endpoints object with typed configurations for users and posts endpoints.
successCriteria: An 'endpoints' constant exists with at least two properties (users and posts), each having a 'url' string and a 'method' literal type that matches EndpointMap.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your object has the correct structure with url and method properties for each endpoint.
steps.feedbackWrong: The endpoints object doesn't match the expected structure. Review the EndpointMap type definition.

steps.title: Create fetch client function signature
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'fetchClient' that accepts a generic type parameter 'K' constrained to keyof EndpointMap, a parameter 'endpoint' of type K, and a parameter 'params' of type EndpointMap[K]['params']. The function should return a Promise of type ApiResponse<EndpointMap[K]['response']>.
steps.hint: Use the generic type parameter 'K extends keyof EndpointMap' to ensure the endpoint name is valid. The params type should match the endpoint's params definition, and the return type should wrap the endpoint's response type in ApiResponse.
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed fetch client function signature is defined with proper generic constraints and parameter types.
successCriteria: The fetchClient function is declared with generic type K constrained to keyof EndpointMap, endpoint parameter of type K, params parameter of type EndpointMap[K]['params'], and returns Promise<ApiResponse<EndpointMap[K]['response']>>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Check that your function uses the generic type K extends keyof EndpointMap, and that the params and return types match the endpoint map structure.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function signature doesn't match the requirements. Review how to use generics with keyof and indexed access types to create type-safe parameters.

steps.title: Implement URL construction logic
steps.instruction: Inside your fetchClient function, add logic to construct the full API URL by combining the endpoint's base URL and path. Use template literals to safely join them.
steps.hint: You can access the endpoint configuration from your endpoints object using the endpointName parameter, then combine its baseUrl and path properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchClient function will have internal logic to build the target URL from the endpoint configuration.
successCriteria: The fetchClient function contains code that constructs a URL by combining the endpoint's baseUrl and path properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're accessing the endpoint configuration from your endpoints object and using template literals to combine baseUrl and path.
steps.feedbackWrong: The URL construction logic is missing or incorrect. Remember to access the endpoint configuration and combine baseUrl and path properties.

steps.instruction: Inside the fetchClient function, create a requestConfig object that includes the HTTP method from the endpoint configuration and sets headers to accept JSON.
steps.hint: Extract the method from the endpoint configuration and create a config object with method and headers properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchClient function should include a requestConfig object with method and headers properties.
successCriteria: A requestConfig object is created inside fetchClient with method from the endpoint configuration and headers set to accept JSON.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your requestConfig includes both method and headers properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The requestConfig object is missing or incomplete. Check that it includes method and headers properties.

steps.title: Review and compile TypeScript
steps.instruction: Run the TypeScript compiler on your code to verify there are no type errors and validate your complete typed fetch client implementation.
steps.hint: You can run the TypeScript compiler using the 'tsc' command in your terminal. Make sure you're in the directory containing your TypeScript file.

tsc your-file.ts
steps.expectedOutcome: The TypeScript compiler should run without errors, confirming your typed fetch client is correctly implemented with proper type safety.
successCriteria: TypeScript compilation completes successfully with zero type errors reported.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You have some type errors to fix. Review the compiler output to identify and correct the issues in your type definitions or implementations.
